brief.interpretation: Read literally: one launch announcement, sent cold to people who have not bought — so it must say what is now available, why it is worth their attention now, and what the single next step is. I read "launch" as the product's general availability, not a feature update to existing users, because the recipients are non-buyers. No segment was pre-marked as this campaign's, so I wrote to the audience the verified research covers: the ops/IT generalist standing up an internal Slack answer-bot over company docs. That reader is solution_aware — they already know this category exists and some of them have already sketched the build — so the email does not explain what an AI assistant is; it says what orqAgent removes from the build and what to do in the next ten minutes. brief.promise: You can have an answer-bot live in Slack over your own handbook documents — configured, not assembled — and see, run by run, which document it answered from and what it cost.
brief.orientation: For this buyer, orqAgent is a hosted place to configure one agent over their own handbook documents and attach it to Slack, with every answer logged as a run, instead of assembling Slack events, a vector store and a model API themselves.
brief.arc: Single email. It opens on the request this reader already has in their queue — an automated responder in the questions channel — names what standing that up actually involves today, then announces that the assembly step is now the product: documents in, Slack out, every answer logged. It closes on the smallest possible first move: one agent, one document set, one channel, tested before anyone else sees it.
brief.sequence_rationale: One email was requested, so the whole campaign has to spend its single open in the right place. The choice was between three arguments: retrieval trust (we can show which chunks were injected), source convenience (Notion and Google Docs sync by OAuth), and the one I picked — the build itself is the thing being removed, and what replaces it is inspectable. I picked it because it is the only one that is simultaneously the reader's verified problem (the same questions asked repeatedly, answers buried in docs), the documented weakness of the route they would otherwise take (low-code orchestration is on record as poorly suited to reliable, latency-sensitive, observable production use), and open ground on the positioning map (per-run analytics and run history is the one territory where this company carries a checkable number and four competitors are ahead of us on breadth, quality, speed, effort, control and security — axes this email never raises). Retrieval trust is the strongest alternative and is listed as such, but leading on it invites a comparison to semantic search that the evidence cannot win; it is better placed as the reason to test than as the reason to open. Pricing is off the page entirely: it is table stakes competitively, and our two published tables disagree, which turns any quoted limit into a trust problem. The email carries no social proof because there is none to carry. That is the constraint doing the most damage here: the single thing you could send us that would most change this campaign is the answer to — which customers or quotes may we name?

emails.belief_shift: Before: an answer-bot over our handbook is a project — I'd have to assemble it, and then I'd own it forever. After: it is a configuration I can stand up over one document set today, watch run by run, and stop if it does not earn its place.
must_not_say: No plan names, prices, credit counts, execution or run limits, and no '55 Sonnet calls' style equivalences — the company's two published pricing tables contradict each other on the Pro plan and on free-tier runs, and a number the reader can disprove in one click costs more than it buys. The next step is the sign-up page; let the page carry the terms.

No claim or implication that retrieval is semantic or embedding-based, and no claim about answer accuracy, deflection rate or hours saved. Retrieval is keyword scoring over roughly 500-token chunks; the honest move is to invite the reader to test it on their own documents, never to assert quality.

No uptime, SLA, SOC 2, encryption, GDPR or security-posture claims. SOC 2 is only in progress, the uptime guarantee is Enterprise-only, and this reader is not running a vendor security review yet — raising it starts a conversation the evidence cannot finish.

No competitor names and no comparison on speed, breadth, model coverage, quality, effort, control or security. The field is ahead of us on every one of those axes; the email loses the moment it invites the comparison.
No customer names, logos, testimonials, user counts, funding or founding story — none exist in the material, and inventing warmth here is the one failure that cannot be repaired later.

Do not state that this reader has already built a bot, already abandoned one, already has a tool in place, or that their documentation runs to any particular length. Their situation is that questions keep coming and a responder has been asked for or considered — keep the build in the conditional ('if you've priced out wiring this yourself').

Do not position this as replacing a workspace AI assistant or knowledge base the company may already pay for. There is nothing in the material that answers 'why add a third thing', so the ask is 'run one agent beside what exists', never 'switch'.

Do not present guardrails, per-client agent configuration, HIPAA compliance or deep domain-specific operational integrations as available capabilities.
